title: Reliability choreography playbook — cross-team oncall orchestration
body:
Purpose:
This is a practical, lightweight playbook for how Site Reliability, Platform, Serving Runtime, and Product teams coordinate on oncall duties, SLO ownership handoffs, and cross-team mitigations so we reduce friction and speed up mitigation time. The framing is "choreography": not a rigid script, but a set of roles, cues, and fallback moves that teams can reliably execute under pressure.

Scope:
- Applies to sev2/sev1 incidents that materially impact customer-facing inference latency or availability across hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Covers SLO alert triggers, initial triage, escalation flow, cross-team handoff protocol, and postmortem triage.
- Excludes experimental infra changes that are not in prod path (they should follow release runbooks).

Guiding principles (short):
- Small team, clear cues: always try to keep the core incident loop to 3 people for first 10 minutes.
- Fastest path to mitigate: prioritize quick customer-facing mitigation, even if temporary, then root cause.
- Honor ownership: SLO owners coordinate but do not block mitigation decisions.
- Explicit fallbacks: when role X is unreachable after 10 minutes, escalate to Y.

High-level choreography (timeline cues):
- 0–5m: Pager fires. Primary oncall acknowledges in Slack channel #incidents and posts single line: "ack @time, initial symptom (latency / error-rate), primary suspect if known."
- 5–15m: Triage cohort = primary oncall + SLO owner + runtime engineer. Confirm scope (single region/cluster vs global). Decide immediate mitigation (route traffic, scale pool, disable feature).
- 15–45m: If mitigation applied, start damage control comms (customer-status page update) and assign someone for root cause. If not contained, escalate to cross-functional war-room with product and infra leads.
- 45m–end: Runbook->postmortem transition, error budget reconciliation, and remediation ticketing.

Roles and cues (who does what):
- Primary oncall (SRE): first ack, run initial diagnostics, trigger mitigation.
- SLO owner (service team): confirm SLO boundaries affected, pull metrics, decide on error budget policy (allow burn, throttle, apply failover).
- Runtime engineer (serving-runtime): investigate model-serving specific telemetry, check KV cache, batching changes, kernel failures.
- Platform infra lead: cluster health, autoscaler decisions, quota adjustments.
- Customer success liaison (CS): drafts external comm if customer-visible.
- Incident commander (IC) — appointed if incident escalates: single decision maker for cross-team tradeoffs until delegated.

Rotation and backup matrix (example schedule):
- Week A: Primary oncall: Aisha (SRE); backup: Evan. SLO owner oncall: Maya (Host API); backup: Ramesh.
- Week B: Primary oncall: Lena; backup: Sofia.
(Actual rotation maintained in ENGOPS-rotation spreadsheet; link in linked_artifacts)

SLO-specific play patterns (examples):
1) Latency SLO breach (p50/p95 elevated):
  - Cue: p95 > target AND trending for 3 minutes.
  - Quick move: reduce batching window, throttle heavy routes, route noncritical traffic to lower SLA tier.
  - Follow: measure tail latency heatmap, enable additional instances if autoscaler slowed.

2) Availability SLO breach (error-rate spike):
  - Cue: error-rate > threshold for 1 minute OR error budget burn > 3% in last 15m.
  - Quick move: failover to alternative region or model variant; if model variant mismatch risk exists, apply rate limit for new requests and return cached responses where possible.
  - Follow: trace sample requests, check kernel OOMs/driver logs.

Communication templates (copy/paste):
- Slack ack (first message):
  "[ack] 2026-02-04T09:12Z — Incident acked by @priya. Symptom: p95 inference latency ~800ms (+300ms from baseline) in us-west1. Initial suspect: batching backlog on pool-3. Coflow: @runtime @platform for triage."

- Status update (customer-friendly):
  "We’re investigating increased latency in inference for some customers in us-west1. We’ve routed traffic and are applying mitigations. We will provide an update in 30 minutes. A subset of requests may see slower responses; no data loss expected."

- Postmortem header:
  "Summary — what happened in plain english. Timeline — minute-by-minute important actions. Impact — affected customers and SLO impact. Root cause — concise. Remediation & follow-ups — who, what, when. Owner for each follow-up."

Runbook snippets (copyable commands & dashboards):
- Quick metrics checks:
  "curl -s 'https://metrics.redwood.internal/api/query?expr=service:inference_latency_p95{region=\"us-west1\"}'"
- Restart a serving pool:
  "kubectl rollout restart deployment/serving-pool-3 -n inference && watch kubectl get pods -l app=serving-pool-3 -n inference"
- Rollback model variant (example):
  "PATCH /api/v1/routes/<route>/target -> body {\"model_variant\":\"v1.2.3\"}"

SLO rollout plan (3-phase):
- Phase 0 (Pilot, 2 weeks): pick 3 services (hosted-api, embeddings, streaming) — validate alert thresholds and sprint runbook.
- Phase 1 (Adopt, 6 weeks): expand to all public routes, instrument dashboards, add error budget dashboards, run two simulated burn drills.
- Phase 2 (Operationalize, ongoing): enshrine ownership in team contracts, integrate SLO checks into PR gating for infra changes.

Quality gates & acceptance criteria for SLO runbooks:
- Runbook accepted when: quick mitigation documented, 2 operators can execute it in <= 10m in a tabletop test, and relevant dashboards populate within 5 minutes of deployment.

Risk register (top items):
- Risk: cascading autoscaler delays causing tail latency spikes. Mitigation: warm standby pools + autoscaler tuning experiments (ENGOPS-1310).
- Risk: ambiguous ownership between product and platform for shared routes. Mitigation: explicit SLO owner assignment in service registry and monthly ownership sync.

Experiment track (what to try next sprint):
- Trial continuous prefix caching for top-10 heavy routes for 2 weeks; measure token-cost delta vs p95 change.
- Canary an adaptive batching profile that shrinks max-batch-size under tail pressure.

Metric dashboard checklist (must-have tiles):
- p50/p95/p99 latency by route and region
- Request-rate by route and model-variant
- Error-rate and error-budget burn rate (1h, 6h, 24h)
- Queue depth and longest-waiting requests in each pool

Postmortem & learning cadence:
- Within 48h: initial RCA draft.
- Within 7 days: final postmortem with remediation tickets and owners.
- Monthly: reliability retro where teams present two incidents and one learning to share cross-org.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- What is the exact error budget policy for Dedicated customers vs Hosted free-tier? (Product ops to decide by 2026-02-10)
- Should we add an automated switch to circuit-break to protect model-serving kernels under memory pressure? (runtime/infra research needed)

Next steps (concrete):
1) Run a tabletop using this choreography on 2026-02-10 with SRE + runtime + platform + product reps. Owner: Priya.
2) Add the two quick runbook snippets to runbooks index (ENGOPS-1299). Owner: Evan.
3) Pilot the Phase 0 SLO rollout for hosted-api next sprint. Owner: Maya.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep playbook lean. Avoid 10-step decision trees that no one reads during a Sev.
- Consider a one-pager "three moves" card for new SREs that summarizes the choreography.

Historical context:
This doc grew out of repeated friction we saw in Q4 2025 where SLO alerts would bounce between product and platform for 20+ minutes while customers saw increased latency. The goal is pragmatic clarity not bureaucracy.

Appendix: quick links
- Incident Slack channel template: #incidents-template
- Runbooks index: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/Reliability/Runbooks
- Rotation spreadsheet: https://sheets.redwood.com/engops/oncall-rotations
